tagline.text: A race festival of the Visayan paraw sailboat across the Iloilo Strait

location.label: Location
location.text: Villa Beach, Arevalo District, Iloilo City

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Late February to early March (dates change each year)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~1,500 (estimated meals and transport, excluding lodging)

children.text: Held since 1973, the Paraw Regatta sends the Visayan double-outrigger sailboat, the paraw, across the Iloilo Strait. A race of about 30 km, a slalom, sail painting and dance contests fill the days, and at dusk lighted paraws brighten the sea.

The Paraw Regatta Festival is a traditional sailboat festival staged at Villa Beach in Arevalo, the westernmost district of Iloilo City. The paraw is a traditional outrigger sailboat of the Visayas: bamboo outriggers on both sides of the hull keep it balanced, and it flies a colorful square sail. The organizers present the event as the oldest traditional sailing race in Asia, and the first regatta took place in

The beginning was modest. Local sailing enthusiasts and cultural advocates, worried that motorboats were pushing the paraw out of use, held a half-day race of fishermen with support from the Department of Tourism. The event later grew into a joint effort of Iloilo City, Oton and the Guimaras municipalities of Jordan and Buenavista, and it is now a multi-day festival with dance, painting, food and beach sports alongside the race. Since 2023 it has been run by the Iloilo Festivals Foundation (IFFI), which also manages Dinagyang and Kasadyahan. Boats are grouped by hull length and sail type. Class 1 is for paraws of about 16 feet or less built strictly with traditional materials and methods, and Class 2 covers about 16 to 22 feet with a wider range of building materials. Painted and unpainted sails are also scored separately. At least 44 boats were reported to have raced in 2025.

The main attraction is the main race. The paraws start off Villa Beach, head north along the coast of mainland Panay, cross the Iloilo Strait, round part of the Guimaras coast and return to Villa Beach. The distance is usually given as about
30km

, and the wind and tides make the course demanding even for seasoned sailors. From the beach, dozens of sails filling the horizon at once is a striking sight. The event is led by the Iloilo City government and the festivals foundation, and side events such as Pinta Tawo (body painting), a miniature paraw race, and rowing and paddling contests are added in many years. Because the program is large, it is easier to pick two or three events you really want to see and plan around them.

The schedule shifts a little every year, so check the official announcements before you go. It was once said to be held on the third weekend of February, but in 2025 and 2026 the main race fell around the first Sunday of March. This is a busy period, so book lodging early and get to the beach early. In 2026, emergency officials counted 2,000 to 2,500 people at the sailing and up to 6,350 across the highlight events, with no major incidents reported.

The centerpiece of the festival starts at Villa Beach, crosses the strait and loops back from the Guimaras side. You can watch the start and the return from the beach, and the finish line is often set up in front of the beachfront restaurants. The course is known for its tricky wind and tides.
A maneuvering race held close to shore about a day before the main race. You can see paraws weaving between buoys at close range, which makes for good photos.

A contest in which sails are painted with artwork. The finished, colorful sails are judged on race day, and a sea full of painted sails looks like an exhibition in itself. In some years a painting event was held at the beachfront restaurant Tatoy's in Arevalo at the start of the festival.
A contest of traditional dance and music. In some years it was staged as a street dance at a downtown venue such as the Iloilo Freedom Grandstand.
On the evening of the main race, paraws hung with lanterns light up the water and fireworks follow. It has a different mood from the daytime race, so it is best to claim a spot before sunset.
A food festival is held during the festival, along with a contest of roast whole pig, or lechon. Villa Beach has a cluster of seafood restaurants, so it is a good place to eat after the race.

Beach football, volleyball and ultimate frisbee tournaments, a miniature paraw race, a fishing contest and rowing competitions take place. The lineup differs a little each year, so check that year's program.
Take Grab or a taxi from downtown Iloilo to Villa Beach in Arevalo. Shade and beach spots fill up early, so it pays to hurry.
Walk along the beach to see the paraws preparing to set out and their colorful sails. Check that year's announcement for the race time.
Have seafood for lunch at the beachfront restaurants and rest while looking out at the sea during the race.
Welcome the paraws coming back and watch the finish. Follow on-site announcements for results and sail judging news.
Watch the lighted paraws and fireworks. Many people leave at once, so think ahead about your ride home.

Event times change every year, so check the latest announcements from the Iloilo City government and the festivals foundation during the festival. The slalom is held about a day before the main race, and in 2026 it was reported to have 17 boats of 25 feet, 17 of 30 feet and 6 of 40 feet.
Stroll the streets and eateries of downtown Iloilo to get into the mood.
Watch the slalom at Villa Beach. It is held close to shore, so you can see the paraws up close.
Head to the beach early to watch the main race.
Finish with the lighted paraws and fireworks.
Flights run from Manila (NAIA) to Iloilo International Airport (ILO) and take a little over
1 hour
. Schedules change often, so check when you book.
Iloilo International Airport is in Cabatuan, and the ride into the city by Grab is reported at about
40-50 minutes
. Getting to Villa Beach takes longer.
During the festival, flights and rooms sell out early, so it is best to book soon.
Villa Beach is in Arevalo District, southwest of Iloilo City, about
6km
from the city center.
Grab or a metered taxi is the easiest way. On festival days the area around the beach is crowded, so you may have to walk in.
From Guimaras, take a boat from Jordan Wharf to Parola Wharf in Iloilo, then go overland to Villa Beach in Arevalo. Check return sailings around the race, when crowds may be heavier.

The festival usually falls from late February to early March. That is Iloilo's dry season, so the weather is fairly stable, but the strait is windy. In 2025, reports said strong winds damaged ten paraws.
The 2026 main race started from Villa Beach in Arevalo on March 1. The usual timing in the
Tourism Promotions Board event listing
can differ from the main race date. Check the organizer’s program for the year you plan to visit.

The festival is counted among the city's signature tourism events along with Dinagyang, Kasadyahan, Chinese New Year celebrations and the Jaro Fiesta. If you visit Iloilo at that time of year, check whether these events overlap.

Villa Beach has resorts and restaurants and bars popular with locals. Among them, Tatoy's and Breakthrough are beachfront seafood restaurants, and in 2026 the finish of the main race was in front of Tatoy's. Seats fill up early during the festival, so ask about reservations.
You can choose between beachside resorts and hotels in downtown Iloilo. Villa Beach is about
6km
from the city center, so plan your day with traffic in mind. Iloilo is rich in local food, so take the chance to try restaurants in the city too.

Arevalo, where Villa Beach lies, is the westernmost district of Iloilo City. A Spanish settlement was established in 1566, and in 1581 Governor Gonzalo Ronquillo de Peñalosa formally founded the town as La Villa Rica de Arévalo. It served as the provincial capital from the early 1580s until 1700. It was annexed into Iloilo City in 1937 and is known today as the Flower Capital of Iloilo for its plant and flower sales. After the race, browsing Arevalo's flower shops is a good way to use your time. In the 2024 census, Arevalo had a population of 57,265.
To watch from the beach, arrive early and stake out shade and a spot on the sand.
Book lodging and flights as soon as the festival dates are announced.
The beach has little shade, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
Dates change every year, so check the official announcements of the Iloilo City government and the festivals foundation first.
Grab may be hard to get when events end, so decide how you will get back in advance.
Adding one more day on Guimaras makes the trip more complete.
Keep your valuables with you and look after your belongings.

For photos, aim separately for daytime, when the painted sails are clearest, and dusk, when the lighted paraws are out. Rely on posted notices and official announcements for the venue guide and timetable.
The strait is windy, so the schedule may change or be suspended depending on the weather. Race dates change every year, so check the latest announcements.
On event days the beach and access roads are crowded and traffic can jam.
When going near the water or boats, follow the organizers' guidance and the instructions of safety staff.
Schedules and programs change every year, and events may be altered or canceled.
Watch out for pickpockets in the crowds.
It is about
6km
from downtown to Villa Beach. The city offers street scenes and local food.
It is about
15 minutes
by pump boat across the strait, and the race course passes along the island. It is a good place to stay one more day and look around.
A riverside promenade in downtown Iloilo City that is pleasant for a walk.
